arguments.i: Asking round one of design tree

questions.question: Key the limit on `x-customer-id` alone, accepting that the header is client-supplied and therefore rotatable?

options.label: Yes — x-customer-id only
options.description: One bucket per customer id, exactly how the API already identifies callers.
options.tradeoff: One counter, per-customer tiering becomes possible, no IP plumbing; a client that rotates the header walks straight past the limit.
options.holds_when: The header is set by a gateway you control, or the goal is containing an accidental 40k spike rather than resisting a determined abuser.
options.cost: One module in src/, a few lines in the POST branch of server.ts.

options.label: Customer id + per-IP ceiling
options.description: Two counters: the customer bucket, plus a coarse per-IP cap.
options.tradeoff: Closes header rotation; doubles the failure and alerting surface and punishes enterprises that share egress NAT.
options.holds_when: Abuse must be resisted now, not just accidental bursts.
options.cost: Two counters, IP extraction that trusts X-Forwarded-For only from the LB, two failure modes to test.

options.label: Client IP only
options.description: Ignore the header for limiting purposes.
options.tradeoff: Unbypassable by header games; kills per-customer tiers and merges unrelated customers behind one NAT.
options.holds_when: You are willing to drop enterprise tiering from this plan.
options.cost: Cheapest limiter, but PLAN.md's tiering branch dies.

brief.where: `src/server.ts:7-8` reads `x-customer-id` straight off the request and 401s when missing; nothing validates it. `PLAN.md:7-10` gives 3 instances behind a round-robin LB and 20 enterprise customers that legitimately burst. The incident was one customer's script at 40k orders in 10 minutes.
brief.what: Whether the limiter keys on the customer header, the client IP, or both. This fixes every downstream decision: per-customer tiers only exist if the customer id is the key, and Retry-After/observability are meaningless without a stable key. Code cannot settle it — it depends on whether you trust the header and whether enterprises share egress addresses.
brief.how: Customer-only → round 2 asks for tier numbers and who owns them. IP-only → that branch is pruned and the plan becomes a blunt flood guard. Both → round 2 also asks for the IP ceiling value and the trusted-proxy rule.

evidence.note: Header read, 401 path, and the POST branch that would get the limiter.
Three instances, round-robin, shared Redis, bursty enterprise integrations.

risks: Header spoofing turns the limit into a speed bump; the real fix is authenticating the caller, which this plan does not do.
Keying on IP behind a round-robin LB without X-Forwarded-For trust makes every request look like the load balancer.

questions.question: Use a token bucket per key (steady refill plus burst capacity) rather than a fixed or sliding window?

options.label: Yes — token bucket (GCRA)
options.description: Refill at a steady rate, allow a burst up to the bucket size.
options.tradeoff: Absorbs the legit enterprise burst and enforces a long-run rate, with no double spend across a window boundary; adds a second number (burst) per tier that nobody has measured yet.
options.holds_when: Legit clients are bursty — which PLAN.md:10 says they are.
options.cost: Two fields per key (tokens, last refill) or one GCRA timestamp; atomic refill-and-take in one Lua script if Redis.

options.label: Fixed window
options.description: Count requests per calendar window, reset on the boundary.
options.tradeoff: Simplest possible counter and cheapest to reason about; allows up to 2x the limit at a window boundary and clamps a legit burst at reset.
options.holds_when: You want the smallest diff this week and can live with 2x spikes.
options.cost: INCR + EXPIRE, no Lua needed.

options.label: Sliding window
options.description: Weighted rolling counter or timestamp log over the last N seconds.
options.tradeoff: Accurate and smooth, no boundary spike; more state per key and bursty clients hit the ceiling more often.
options.holds_when: Fairness matters more than admitting bursts.
options.cost: Timestamp list or two-window weighting; more Redis ops per request.

brief.where: No limiter exists anywhere in the repo. `src/orders.ts:10-13` shows POST /orders is a single Postgres insert per call, so the cost is linear in request count. `PLAN.md:10` says 20 enterprise customers legitimately burst.
brief.what: Which algorithm. This is a decision, not a lookup: the burst requirement rules out the burst-hostile options, but the cost of a second tunable parameter is yours. The choice also fixes what Retry-After can honestly say.
brief.how: Token bucket → round 2 asks for rate and burst per tier and how Retry-After is computed (time to one token vs time to full bucket). Fixed window → Retry-After is seconds to reset. Sliding window → Retry-After from the oldest timestamp.

evidence.note: The expensive call the limiter protects.
POST is expensive; 20 enterprise integrations legitimately burst.

risks: Burst capacity is an unmeasured second knob; set too low it throttles the integrations you promised not to break, too high it admits the next 40k spike.

questions.question: Keep counters in the existing Redis cluster, in a separate keyspace with short TTLs, instead of per-instance memory?

options.label: Yes — Redis, namespaced
options.description: Shared counters across all 3 instances, key prefix like rl:, TTLs on every key.
options.tradeoff: Global limit across 3 instances and limits tunable without a deploy; adds a network hop to every POST and shares fate with another service's sessions.
options.holds_when: The limit must mean the same thing on all three instances.
options.cost: Redis client, atomic Lua or single-command refill, 1-2ms per POST, plus ops for key naming and timeout.

options.label: Per-instance memory
options.description: A Map in each Bun process.
options.tradeoff: No new dependency, no latency, cannot fail; the effective limit is 3x what you configure, resets on deploy, and cannot be tuned per customer without a restart.
options.holds_when: You accept roughly 3x the intended limit and only need a coarse flood guard this week.
options.cost: Smallest diff; a cleanup timer and an eviction policy for unbounded customer ids.

brief.where: Three instances behind a round-robin LB (`PLAN.md:7`); a Redis 7 cluster already serves sessions for another service (`PLAN.md:8`). No Redis client exists in the repo today — `src/db.ts` only wraps Postgres.
brief.what: Where counters live. This decides whether the configured limit is a real limit or a per-instance one, and whether rejection is a new failure mode. Memory cannot answer the shared-accounting question at all; Redis can, at the cost of a dependency in the request path.
brief.how: Redis → round 2 asks fail-open vs fail-closed, timeout budget, and key naming/TTL. Memory → round 2 instead asks the per-instance divisor story and drops the store-down question.

evidence.note: Instance count and the shared Redis cluster.
Only Postgres is wired up; no Redis client yet.

risks: Sharing the sessions cluster means a limiter bug — hot key, KEYS scan, large pipeline — degrades login for another service.
A Redis round trip in front of every POST is a new tail-latency contributor and a new outage mode.

questions.question: Limit only `POST /orders` this week, leaving `GET /orders` unmetered?

options.label: Yes — POST only
options.description: One bucket per customer, applied in the POST branch.
options.tradeoff: Targets the expensive call and the actual incident, one integration point, no risk to dashboards and pollers; leaves a cheap but unbounded read path.
options.holds_when: The incident was writes, as PLAN.md:9-10 says.
options.cost: One call site in server.ts:10-13.

options.label: POST plus a loose GET limit
options.description: Second, much higher bucket for reads.
options.tradeoff: Caps a pathological poller too; a second bucket per customer and a second set of numbers to own, with real risk to legit dashboards.
options.holds_when: You have seen read amplification, not just write spikes.
options.cost: Two buckets, two configs, two rejection paths.

options.label: Every route, one shared bucket
options.description: All requests draw from one counter.
options.tradeoff: Simplest mental model for clients; a polling dashboard eats the budget that order creation needs.
options.holds_when: You want a single global fairness number per customer.
options.cost: One bucket, but the limit now conflates reads and writes.

brief.where: `src/server.ts:10-15` has the two handlers: POST inserts through `createOrder`, GET reads through `listOrders`. `PLAN.md:9` states POST is the expensive call, GET cheap.
brief.what: Which routes the limiter wraps. This is not inferable from the code — both are per-customer and both are cheap to wrap; what differs is the blast radius on 20 scripted integrations that may poll.
brief.how: POST only → round 2 tunes a single rate. More routes → round 2 needs per-route numbers and a story for shared vs separate budgets.

evidence.note: The two handlers a middleware would wrap.
POST is the expensive call; enterprises burst legitimately.

risks: An unthrottled GET can still exhaust DB connections and file descriptors under a pathological poller.

questions.question: Reject with `429`, a rounded-up `Retry-After` in seconds, a JSON body `{error:"rate_limited", retryAfterMs}`, and `RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset` headers — never `503`?

options.label: Yes — 429 + Retry-After + JSON + RateLimit headers
options.description: Standard, retry-library friendly, self-describing.
options.tradeoff: Every mainstream SDK and retry middleware honours it, and Remaining lets integrations self-pace; more surface to keep consistent, and the body shape becomes a contract.
options.holds_when: Clients are scripted integrations that can read headers — PLAN.md:10 says they are.
options.cost: A small helper plus header formatting; docs for the 20 customers.

options.label: 429, headers only, no body
options.description: Status and RateLimit headers, empty body.
options.tradeoff: Nothing to version, minimal; clients must parse headers to know when to retry, and your codebase's own JSON error convention is broken.
options.holds_when: Clients are already header-aware.
options.cost: Cheapest.

options.label: 429 without Retry-After
options.description: Bare status.
options.tradeoff: Simplest for you; retry libraries fall back to their own backoff and the 40k script keeps hammering.
options.holds_when: Never, given the incident.
options.cost: Zero, and zero protection against retry storms.

brief.where: `src/server.ts:8` returns a plain-text 401; lines 12 and 15 return JSON. There is no error helper and no existing error envelope to inherit.
brief.what: The client-visible contract on rejection. 20 scripted integrations will branch on whatever you choose; 5xx signals outage and invites aggressive retries, 429 with Retry-After is what retry libraries honour. Whether Retry-After is integer seconds or milliseconds is a decision, not a fact, and changing it later breaks parsers.
brief.how: This fixes the shape round 2 must fill: Retry-After precision comes from the algorithm, and the exact header set becomes the customer-facing doc.

evidence.note: Existing error and success response styles, and where a rejection would be produced.

risks: Retry-After rounded down to 0 produces hot-loop retries that look like the original incident.
A JSON body you later change breaks clients that sniff it.

questions.question: Ship behind a `RATE_LIMIT_MODE=shadow|enforce` switch, run shadow for about a day to collect real rates, then enforce with generous first-pass limits?

options.label: Yes — shadow then enforce
options.description: Count and log decisions without rejecting; flip a flag to enforce.
options.tradeoff: Zero customer risk on first deploy and it produces the per-customer data that tiers need; adds a flag, a log line, and a step someone must actually perform.
options.holds_when: You want the tier numbers to come from observed traffic rather than guesses.
options.cost: One env flag, one structured log line per POST, an owner and a date for the flip.

options.label: Enforce on first deploy, generous limits
options.description: Pick high numbers, reject immediately.
options.tradeoff: Protects the DB from day one; every wrong guess is a dropped order and you learn the real rates from rejections.
options.holds_when: The incident is still live and you cannot wait a day.
options.cost: No flag; rollback is a redeploy of the previous build.

options.label: Enforce but exempt the 20 enterprise customers
options.description: Hard enforce for everyone not on a list.
options.tradeoff: Protects the DB while keeping the promised integrations intact; needs the customer list and turns the limiter into a two-class system from day one.
options.holds_when: You can produce the list of 20 accounts today.
options.cost: An allowlist or high tier seeded from a hand-written list, plus a review process for who gets added.

brief.where: Repo has no tests, no package.json, no config layer — only `src/server.ts`, `orders.ts`, `db.ts`. `PLAN.md:20` lists rollout as undecided and PLAN.md:3 wants it shipped this week.
brief.what: Whether the first deploy is allowed to reject traffic. Limits are unmeasured, so enforcing immediately converts a guess into customer-visible failures; shadow mode buys data at the cost of one deferral. Whether 'this week' is hard changes which side of the trade you can afford.
brief.how: Shadow → round 2 needs the flip criterion and the per-customer rates to set tiers. Immediate enforce → round 2 needs limit values now and an exemption policy. Allowlist → round 2 needs the list's ownership.

evidence.note: Ship this week, bursty enterprises, rollout undecided.
The entire server; there is no config or flag mechanism to piggyback on.

risks: A shadow flag nobody flips leaves the DB unprotected while looking done.
An allowlist becomes permanent and unowned, and the next abusive account is one of the 20.

evidence.note: Header read, 401 path, and the POST branch that would get the limiter.
Three instances, round-robin, shared Redis, bursty enterprise integrations.

brief.how: Customer-only → round 2 asks for tier numbers and who owns them. IP-only → that branch is pruned and the plan becomes a blunt flood guard. Both → round 2 also asks for the IP ceiling value and the trusted-proxy rule.
risks: Header spoofing turns the limit into a speed bump; the real fix is authenticating the caller, which this plan does not do.
Keying on IP behind a round-robin LB without X-Forwarded-For trust makes every request look like the load balancer.
brief.what: Whether the limiter keys on the customer header, the client IP, or both. This fixes every downstream decision: per-customer tiers only exist if the customer id is the key. Code cannot settle it — it depends on whether you trust the header and whether enterprises share egress addresses.
brief.where: `src/server.ts:7-8` reads `x-customer-id` straight off the request and 401s when missing; nothing validates it. `PLAN.md:7-10` gives 3 instances behind a round-robin LB and 20 enterprise customers that legitimately burst. The incident was one customer's script at 40k orders in 10 minutes.

options.cost: One module in src/, a few lines in the POST branch of server.ts.
options.description: One bucket per customer id, exactly how the API already identifies callers.
options.holds_when: The header is set by a gateway you control, or the goal is containing an accidental 40k spike rather than resisting a determined abuser.
options.label: Yes — x-customer-id only
options.tradeoff: One counter, per-customer tiering becomes possible, no IP plumbing; a client that rotates the header walks straight past the limit.

options.cost: Two counters, IP extraction that trusts X-Forwarded-For only from the LB, two failure modes to test.
options.description: Two counters: the customer bucket, plus a coarse per-IP cap.
options.holds_when: Abuse must be resisted now, not just accidental bursts.
options.label: Customer id + per-IP ceiling
options.tradeoff: Closes header rotation; doubles the failure and alerting surface and punishes enterprises that share egress NAT.

options.cost: Cheapest limiter, but PLAN.md's tiering branch dies.
options.description: Ignore the header for limiting purposes.
options.holds_when: You are willing to drop enterprise tiering from this plan.
options.label: Client IP only
options.tradeoff: Unbypassable by header games; kills per-customer tiers and merges unrelated customers behind one NAT.

questions.question: Key the limit on `x-customer-id` alone, accepting that the header is client-supplied and therefore rotatable?

evidence.note: The expensive call the limiter protects.
POST is expensive; 20 enterprise integrations legitimately burst.

brief.how: Token bucket → round 2 asks for rate and burst per tier and how Retry-After is computed (time to one token vs time to full bucket). Fixed window → Retry-After is seconds to reset. Sliding window → Retry-After from the oldest timestamp.
risks: Burst capacity is an unmeasured second knob; set too low it throttles the integrations you promised not to break, too high it admits the next 40k spike.
brief.what: Which algorithm. This is a decision, not a lookup: the burst requirement rules out the burst-hostile options, but the cost of a second tunable parameter is yours. The choice also fixes what Retry-After can honestly say.
brief.where: No limiter exists anywhere in the repo. `src/orders.ts:10-13` shows POST /orders is a single Postgres insert per call, so the cost is linear in request count. `PLAN.md:10` says 20 enterprise customers legitimately burst.

options.cost: Two fields per key (tokens, last refill) or one GCRA timestamp; atomic refill-and-take in one Lua script if Redis.
options.description: Refill at a steady rate, allow a burst up to the bucket size.
options.holds_when: Legit clients are bursty — which PLAN.md:10 says they are.
options.label: Yes — token bucket (GCRA)
options.tradeoff: Absorbs the legit enterprise burst and enforces a long-run rate, with no double spend across a window boundary; adds a second number (burst) per tier that nobody has measured yet.

options.cost: INCR + EXPIRE, no Lua needed.
options.description: Count requests per calendar window, reset on the boundary.
options.holds_when: You want the smallest diff this week and can live with 2x spikes.
options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Simplest possible counter and cheapest to reason about; allows up to 2x the limit at a window boundary and clamps a legit burst at reset.

options.cost: Timestamp list or two-window weighting; more Redis ops per request.
options.description: Weighted rolling counter or timestamp log over the last N seconds.
options.holds_when: Fairness matters more than admitting bursts.
options.label: Sliding window
options.tradeoff: Accurate and smooth, no boundary spike; more state per key and bursty clients hit the ceiling more often.

questions.question: Use a token bucket per key (steady refill plus burst capacity) rather than a fixed or sliding window?

evidence.note: Instance count and the shared Redis cluster.
Only Postgres is wired up; no Redis client yet.

brief.how: Redis → round 2 asks fail-open vs fail-closed, timeout budget, and key naming/TTL. Memory → round 2 instead asks the per-instance divisor story and drops the store-down question.
risks: Sharing the sessions cluster means a limiter bug — hot key, KEYS scan, large pipeline — degrades login for another service.
A Redis round trip in front of every POST is a new tail-latency contributor and a new outage mode.
brief.what: Where counters live. This decides whether the configured limit is a real limit or a per-instance one, and whether rejection is a new failure mode. Memory cannot answer the shared-accounting question at all; Redis can, at the cost of a dependency in the request path.
brief.where: Three instances behind a round-robin LB (`PLAN.md:7`); a Redis 7 cluster already serves sessions for another service (`PLAN.md:8`). No Redis client exists in the repo today — `src/db.ts` only wraps Postgres.

options.cost: Redis client, atomic Lua or single-command refill, 1-2ms per POST, plus ops for key naming and timeout.
options.description: Shared counters across all 3 instances, key prefix like rl:, TTLs on every key.
options.holds_when: The limit must mean the same thing on all three instances.
options.label: Yes — Redis, namespaced
options.tradeoff: Global limit across 3 instances and limits tunable without a deploy; adds a network hop to every POST and shares fate with another service's sessions.

options.cost: Smallest diff; a cleanup timer and an eviction policy for unbounded customer ids.
options.description: A Map in each Bun process.
options.holds_when: You accept roughly 3x the intended limit and only need a coarse flood guard this week.
options.label: Per-instance memory
options.tradeoff: No new dependency, no latency, cannot fail; the effective limit is 3x what you configure, resets on deploy, and cannot be tuned per customer without a restart.

questions.question: Keep counters in the existing Redis cluster, in a separate keyspace with short TTLs, instead of per-instance memory?

risks: An unthrottled GET can still exhaust DB connections and file descriptors under a pathological poller.

options.cost: One call site in server.ts:10-13.

options.holds_when: The incident was writes, as PLAN.md:9-10 says.

options.cost: One bucket, but the limit now conflates reads and writes.
options.description: All requests draw from one counter.
options.holds_when: You want a single global fairness number per customer.
options.label: Every route, one shared bucket

options.description: Standard, retry-library friendly, self-describing.

options.label: Yes — 429 + Retry-After + JSON + RateLimit headers

options.cost: Cheapest.
options.description: Status and RateLimit headers, empty body.
options.holds_when: Clients are already header-aware.
options.label: 429, headers only, no body
options.tradeoff: Nothing to version, minimal; clients must parse headers to know when to retry, and your codebase's own JSON error convention is broken.

options.cost: Zero, and zero protection against retry storms.
options.description: Bare status.
options.holds_when: Never, given the incident.
options.label: 429 without Retry-After
options.tradeoff: Simplest for you; retry libraries fall back to their own backoff and the 40k script keeps hammering.

evidence.note: Ship this week, and the scale of the incident.
Bursty enterprises you must not break.

options.cost: One env flag, one structured log line per POST, an owner and a date for the flip.
options.description: Count and log decisions without rejecting; flip a flag to enforce.
options.holds_when: You want the tier numbers to come from observed traffic rather than guesses.
options.label: Yes — shadow then enforce
options.tradeoff: Zero customer risk on first deploy and it produces the per-customer data that tiers need; adds a flag, a log line, and a step someone must actually perform.

options.description: Pick high numbers, reject immediately.
options.holds_when: The incident is still live and you cannot wait a day.

options.description: Hard enforce for everyone not on a list.
options.holds_when: You can produce the list of 20 accounts today.
options.label: Enforce but exempt the 20 enterprise customers
options.tradeoff: Protects the DB while keeping the promised integrations intact; needs the customer list and turns the limiter into a two-class system from day one.

args.i: Asking round two of design tree

evidence.note: Three instances, shared Redis cluster.
The only revenue path; every rejected request here is a lost order.

brief.how: Fail-open-with-fallback → round 3 needs only the alert threshold. Hard fail-open → round 3 needs the alert and accepts unbounded writes. Fail-closed → round 3 needs a customer-comms plan for Redis blips.
risks: Hard fail-open recreates the original incident whenever Redis hiccups.
Fail-closed converts a Redis blip into a total order-creation outage for all customers.
The fallback bucket is per instance, so during an outage the real ceiling is roughly 3x the configured limit — acceptable only because it is bounded.
brief.what: Policy when the counter store errors or exceeds its timeout. Code cannot decide this: it is a choice between a bounded write flood and refusing revenue. Note the two sub-decisions folded in: the timeout budget (50ms) and whether a rejected request consumes a token (it must not).
brief.where: Redis is now the chosen store (`PLAN.md:8`) and no Redis client exists in the repo yet. `src/server.ts:10-13` is the revenue path: the limiter sits in front of the Postgres insert in `src/orders.ts:12`.

options.cost: Second backend for the same GCRA logic behind one interface; ~30 lines plus a test seam.
options.description: On Redis error or timeout, enforce the same limits from a per-instance in-memory bucket.
options.holds_when: You want a bounded ceiling even when the shared store is gone.
options.label: Yes — degrade to a per-instance bucket
options.tradeoff: Bounded rather than unbounded during an outage, reusing the algorithm you already have; during the outage the effective ceiling is about 3x the configured limit and resets on deploy.

options.cost: Three lines: log, increment a counter, return allow.
options.description: Log and alert, allow every request.
options.holds_when: Redis availability is high and an outage is genuinely rare.
options.label: Fail open — allow, alert loudly
options.tradeoff: No customer is ever blocked by our infrastructure; a Redis outage silently restores the unprotected 40k-order behaviour.

options.cost: Rejection path plus comms; simplest code of the three.
options.description: Reject with 503 while the store is unavailable.
options.holds_when: Protecting Postgres outranks accepting orders.
options.label: Fail closed — reject
options.tradeoff: The database is protected absolutely; one Redis blip is a full outage for all 20 enterprise integrations.

questions.question: On Redis error or timeout, fall back to a per-instance in-memory bucket with the same limits rather than allowing everything or rejecting everything?

evidence.note: Postgres wrapper already exists and is the app's own database.
Twenty enterprise customers who legitimately burst — the accounts that will need exceptions.
Tiering and ownership are explicitly undecided.

brief.how: Postgres overrides → round 3 sets the numbers and the flip criterion, and needs an on-call runbook for raising one customer. Repo config → round 3 includes a deploy step in the rollout. Redis config → round 3 must cover what happens to limits during a Redis outage.
risks: A config-file mechanism makes every false positive a deploy, which is exactly when you have least time.
Storing limits in Redis means the store outage also removes your ability to fix limits.
A DB read per request adds a second network dependency to the POST path.
brief.what: Where the numbers live, who can change them and how fast. This is a process decision disguised as a format: a wrong limit at 02:00 must be fixable without a deploy, and the 20 enterprise accounts must have an identifiable owner. It does not fix the values themselves.
brief.where: No config layer exists anywhere in the repo — `src/server.ts` has no flags and no env reads besides `DATABASE_URL` in `db.ts:4`. Postgres is already available to the app.

options.cost: One table, a 10-second per-instance cache, and a rule that support edits rows while platform owns defaults.
options.description: Defaults per tier in env; per-customer overrides in a Postgres table read through a short cache.
options.holds_when: False positives must be fixable within a minute without shipping code.
options.label: Yes — Postgres overrides, platform owns defaults
options.tradeoff: Limits changeable in seconds by support with an audit trail in the table, and defaults still versioned with the code; adds a cached DB read and a second place limits can be wrong.

options.cost: One JSON file in the repo, parsed at boot; changes need a PR and a deploy.
options.description: A checked-in config file: default limit plus per-customer overrides.
options.holds_when: Changes are rare and reviewed changes are the point.
options.label: Config file in the repo
options.tradeoff: Fully versioned, reviewable, zero runtime dependency; a customer hitting a false positive waits for a deploy, which is the worst possible latency.

options.cost: Redis hash reads on the request path, or a local cache of Redis config.
options.description: Defaults and overrides in a Redis hash the limiter reads.
options.holds_when: You accept Redis as both the counter store and the config store.
options.label: Redis-held config
options.tradeoff: Instant changes with no DB or deploy; Redis now also owns your ability to correct limits, and there are two sources of truth.

questions.question: Put per-customer overrides in Postgres with a short cache, defaults in env, and give platform the defaults and support the override list?

evidence.note: Redis 7 shared with another service's sessions — the blast radius being decided.
Only Postgres is wired; Redis access does not exist yet.

brief.how: Dedicated ACL user → ops creates a user restricted to the prefix before the shadow deploy. Prefix-only → round 3 needs a key-collision audit against the sessions service. Separate cluster → round 3 needs provisioning time, and this week's ship may slip.
risks: Shared credentials let a limiter bug — a wrong key, a SCAN, a big pipeline — touch session data and log the whole platform out.
A hot key for a large customer can saturate a single Redis Cluster slot and affect unrelated tenants on it.
brief.what: How isolated the limiter's Redis footprint is. Redis 7 supports ACL users, so 'dedicated credentials' is available, but creating one is an ops task with lead time. 'Separate cluster' is safest and slowest.
brief.where: `PLAN.md:8` says the Redis 7 cluster is already used for sessions by another service; Redis access is not wired into this app at all yet (only Postgres in `src/db.ts`).

options.cost: Ops ticket for an ACL user; one key builder and a TTL rule.
options.description: ACL user limited to `rl:*`, TTL = time to refill the bucket, one EVAL per POST, no SCAN.
options.holds_when: You must not risk another service's sessions.
options.label: Yes — dedicated ACL user plus prefix
options.tradeoff: A limiter bug cannot read or delete session keys, and TTLs free idle customers automatically; needs an ops ticket and a prefix-collision check.

options.cost: Zero ops work today.
options.description: Use the existing session credentials with an `rl:` prefix.
options.tradeoff: Ships fastest; the same credential that reads sessions can be used to delete them by any bug or leaked secret.
options.holds_when: Ops turnaround makes an ACL user impossible this week.
options.label: Shared credentials, prefix only

options.cost: New infrastructure, new connection config, provisioning lead time.
options.description: A separate Redis instance dedicated to limiting.
options.tradeoff: Zero blast radius on sessions and independent failure; most work, and the ship date is at the mercy of provisioning.
options.holds_when: Sessions and rate limiting must not share fate.
options.label: Separate Redis instance

questions.question: Ask ops for a dedicated Redis ACL user restricted to an `rl:*` keyspace, with a TTL equal to the bucket refill time on every the key?

evidence.note: Current plain-text error and JSON success responses; the rejection must fit here.

brief.how: This fixes the doc you hand the 20 customers and the header builder in code. Round 3 only fills in the numeric values.
risks: Retry-After rounded down to 0 causes hot-loop retries that reproduce the incident.
Emitting headers in shadow mode lets a well-behaved client pre-emptively slow itself down before you have decided the limits.
brief.what: The exact header family, the rounding of Retry-After, and whether shadow mode advertises anything. For GCRA, 'one token' and 'bucket full' are different times, so Reset and Retry-After mean different things and must be documented as such.
brief.where: The rejection shape is settled (429, JSON, RateLimit headers); `src/server.ts:8` shows the current plain-text error style. No header helper exists.

options.cost: One helper plus customer docs.
options.description: Draft-style `RateLimit-*`, Retry-After = ceil seconds to the next token with a floor of 1, Reset = seconds until the bucket refills.
options.holds_when: Clients can read headers and you want one standard family.
options.label: Yes — `RateLimit-*`, ceil, floor 1s, no headers in shadow
options.tradeoff: Unambiguous, honest retry timing that never returns 0; fewer clients parse `RateLimit-*` than the legacy `X-` names.

options.cost: Same helper, different names.
options.description: GitHub-style `X-RateLimit-*` headers.
options.tradeoff: The widest client compatibility, because most SDKs already parse it; the names are not the current draft and you inherit their slightly different Reset semantics.
options.holds_when: Your integrations were built against GitHub-style limits.
options.label: `X-RateLimit-*`

options.cost: Two header families, one doc that must explain both.
options.description: Emit both families.
options.tradeoff: Maximum compatibility; duplicated values that can drift apart, and twice the surface in every test.
options.holds_when: You cannot find out what the 20 integrations parse.
options.label: Both families

questions.question: Use draft-style `RateLimit-*` headers, Retry-After as ceil-seconds to the next token with a 1-second floor, Reset as time to a full bucket, and emit no limit headers at all in shadow mode?

evidence.note: The entire server, with no test scaffolding around it.
The insertion that must not double-fire when the limiter and the write race.

brief.how: Tests → the shadow flip gets evidence from deterministic cases, and round 3's flip criterion can rely on them. No tests → the flip criterion rests entirely on observed shadow traffic.
risks: Without a store seam the fail-open path is only exercised in production.
A test that mocks the Postgres insert proves nothing about double-fire; only a real request through server.ts does.
brief.what: The verification bar before flipping to enforce. There is no test framework configured and no package.json; Bun's runner discovers `*.test.ts` without a package.json, so the choice is about seams and scope, not tooling. Also settles limiter placement: before `await req.json()` so rejected requests cost no parsing.
brief.where: Repo has no tests, no package.json, no CI config — only `src/server.ts`, `orders.ts`, `db.ts`.

options.cost: One test file plus a store interface; no build config changes.
options.description: `src/ratelimit.test.ts` run by `bun test`, with a fake store and injected clock, plus one smoke run of the real server.
options.holds_when: You want the token math and fail-open path proven before customers see 429s.
options.label: Yes — bun test, fake store, injected clock
options.tradeoff: Deterministic proof of refill, burst, fail-open and header values without Redis or Postgres; a small refactor to inject the store and clock, and the tests live in src/.

options.cost: Adds package.json and a scripts entry; same tests.
options.description: package.json with `bun test`, same tests.
options.tradeoff: A conventional entry point and a place for future scripts; a new file at the root for a project that currently has none.
options.holds_when: You expect more tooling soon.
options.label: package.json plus the same tests

options.cost: Zero code, zero tests.
options.description: Rely on shadow-mode logs and manual checks.
options.tradeoff: Fastest to ship; token-math and fail-open bugs surface only as customer-visible throttling.
options.holds_when: The incident is still ongoing and shipping outranks verification.
options.label: Shadow logs only
